title: Calls for Army college inquiry after reports of rape and abuse
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCharlotte Hadfield and Sima KotechaSenior UK correspondent Warning: This article contains sexual language and details of s
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCharlotte Hadfield and Sima KotechaSenior UK correspondent Warning: This article contains sexual language and details of sexual assaultCalls are growing for an independent inquiry into an Army training college for teenagers following allegations of rape and sexual abuse against female recruits.Four young women told the BBC they were sexually assaulted and harassed while attending the Army Foundation College (AFC) at Harrogate in North Yorkshire.They described a culture of misogyny and sexual violence at the college, which they all attended when they were 17.Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.The review, which took evidence from over 4,200 women, reported cases of rape, sexual exploitation of under 18s, and women being drugged before being assaulted. It concluded that women were being "denied justice" by a "woefully inadequate" military complaints process.Speaking to the BBC on Thursday, Atherton said: "Concerns at AFC Harrogate were raised years ago, and subsequent data and complaints suggest the problems continued without adequate action".An independent inquiry, she said, was "the best way to establish the facts, restore public confidence and ensure the Army can recruit and retain the talented young people it needs"."Parents, staff and recruits deserve clear answers, accountability where necessary, and confidence that every possible lesson has been learned," she added.Image caption, AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-18s in the UKLewell, who sits on the Defence Committee, said: "I think as a matter of urgency there should be an independent inquiry into the college led by someone with significant safeguarding experience, and they need to be able to speak to the children there."There's been an ongoing culture of what there's been ongoing complaints for a long time now around sexual assault, bullying, sexual abuse, physical abuse so it's a matter of urgency."The Army said "unacceptable and criminal behaviour has absolutely no place in our Armed Forces" as it called for victims and witnesses of criminal behaviour at the college to come forward.It said several reforms had been introduced to support victims, including the Defence Serious Crime Command providing specialist support through the justice process - outside of the Army chain of command.AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act  request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data. Image caption, "He stood against the door so I couldn't get out," Monica tells Sima KotechaThe women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room."They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to. "And then I was raped… by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training. Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of AFC staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."The Army told the BBC a visit to AFC by the Children's Commissioner and safeguarding authorities in January 2026 had recognised "the culture of care and the confidence junior soldiers have in raising concerns".It added that the college's "robust discipline system" has been graded "outstanding" by the schools' inspectorate, Ofsted, which visits the college every three years.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Gunner Jaysley Beck, who was not at AFC, was found dead five months after a 43-year-old officer pinned her down and tried to kiss herAn MoD report last year found that 67% of women in the armed forces had experienced at least one sexualised behaviour in the previous 12 months, compared to 34% of men.Last year, an ex-army sergeant major was jailed for six months for sexually assaulting a 19-year-old soldier, who later took her own life.Warrant Officer Michael Webber, 43, pinned down Royal Artillery Gunner Jaysley Beck and tried to kiss her in July 2021. She was found dead five months later in her barracks at Larkhill, Wiltshire.The inquest into her death ruled the sexual assault and the Army's failure to take appropriate action "more than minimally" contributed to her taking her life.Jaysley's mother, Leighann McCready, told BBC Breakfast Jaysley was 19 when she reported what happened to her chain of command, but she was "disbelieved" and branded "a female trouble maker"."This is the problem that soldiers are facing - what they are going to be branded afterwards," her mother said."If a junior solider can follow their policies and procedures then those above should do exactly the same. Had they had done, I believe our daughter would have still been alive", she added.AFC remains committed to creating a professional, supportive, and safe environment for all recruits, the Army said.It added: "Any suggestion otherwise contradicts the values of respect and inclusivity that we stand for."If you have more information about this story, you can reach Sima by email at Sima.Kotecha@bbc.co.uk

schema.headline: Calls for Army college inquiry after reports of rape and abuse

title: Ukraine hits two oil refineries deep in Russian territory
description: Both Russia and Ukraine have in recent weeks intensified attacks on major cities, energy facilities and warehouses, as the vast front line remains vir
body: Both Russia and Ukraine have in recent weeks intensified attacks on major cities, energy facilities and warehouses, as the vast front line remains virtually static and all mediation efforts to end the war have brought no breakthrough.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Zelensky said on Thursday that the struck Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Russia's Bashkortostan republic was about 1,300km (808 miles) from the Ukrainian border, whereas Slavneft-Yanos was almost 700km (435 miles) away.The Ukrainian president also said that "two military patrol boats and shadow fleet vessels were hit" in the Black Sea, referring to tankers used by Russia to illegally export sanctioned oil."Russia must choose peace," Zelensky said, adding that Ukrainian attacks were "strengthening chances for diplomacy".Evraev said 93 drones were shot down over Yaroslavl region overnight. "Falling debris hit the oil refinery's storage tanks. Emergency services are working to extinguish the fire," he said.BBC Verify confirmed multiple videos and images shared on social media showing huge smoke plumes rising from the refinery.In one of the verified images there appear to be at least four fires at the site.Energy-generating infrastructure in Yaroslavl has been targeted a number of times by Ukraine.The authorities in Bashkortostan have not publicly commented on the reported Ukrainian attack on the Bashneft-Novoil refinery on 5 August.In Ukraine, three people were killed in the town of Balakliya, Kharkiv region, in an overnight Russian drone attack, the country's state emergencies service DSNS said.It said private residential houses were targeted, with fires reported in two buildings.Kharkiv regional head Oleh Synehubov later said that another two people were killed when drones attacked the train station in Lozova. Another eight people were injured.Later on Thursday, five people were killed in Russian strikes on the central Dnipropetrovsk region, local officials said.In the south, the entire city of Kherson is now without electricity after a "critical infrastructure facility" was hit overnight, regional head Oleksandr Prokudin said.In Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa, one person was killed when Russia hit two dry cargo ships.Meanwhile, the Russian military said its forces intercepted or shot down 605 Ukrainian drones overnight over a number of regions.In its latest operational update, the military said it struck Ukraine's fuel, energy and transport facilities, as well as drone storage sites.Additional reporting by Peter Mwai and Richard Irvine-Brown

schema.headline: Ukraine hits two oil refineries deep in Russian territory

title: Iran says deal with Oman on Strait of Hormuz is 'in final stages'
description: Iran says it has reached an agreement with Oman on a route for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei did not
body: Iran says it has reached an agreement with Oman on a route for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei did not give any further details on the agreement, which he said was "in the final stages".Baqaei warned, however, that a deal with Oman would not guarantee safe navigation through the strait, arguing security remained impacted by the US blockade of Iran's ports. The US and Oman have not commented on the proposal.Since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, Tehran has largely blocked the Strait of Hormuz through which about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas usually passes.On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump warned that Iran would be "hit very hard" if the strait did not open "very soon".His comments came after senior US officials said talks had progressed to allow shipments to potentially resume later this week, though Iran has maintained that it is not negotiating with the US and has no plans to do so.Reopening the strait has been a key point in discussions between the two countries and mediators.In his statement, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesman said the "geographical coordinates of the route" had been agreed with Oman."The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States, particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests," he said, according to Iran's official Irna news agency.Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi later told Irna the new route would be temporary and could stay open from two to four months. He did not give further details.Oil prices edged lower on Thursday, with global benchmark Brent crude down by 0.3% at $79.24 (£58.84) in morning Asian trade. Energy prices have fluctuated wildly during the conflict as shipments through the key route for around 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) have been severely disrupted.Since the beginning of the war, traffic through the strait has dwindled. Iran has said all passage needs to be cleared beforehand - and it has attacked vessels which have ignored the order.One of the main points of disagreement between Tehran and Washington has been Iran's threat to impose a fee on vessels wishing to cross the strait. Iran is seeking fees of between 5% and 7% of the price of cargoes from ships using the strait, according to a senior Iranian official cited by Reuters. Oman is discussing fees of around 3%, while Washington wants no fees at all.The proposed deal would also give Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.In June, Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), aiming to stop fighting, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and reach agreement to end the war within 60 days.The deal quickly fell through, as did diplomatic talks, with tit-for-tat attacks resuming just days after the MoU was signed.The US has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports in the region, while another blockade is in place on Saudi Arabia's ports in the Red Sea, imposed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since 20 July.The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel and US-allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's then Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in that first attack, after which he was succeeded by his son Mojtaba Khamenei.The younger Khamenei was wounded in the same strikes that launched the war and has not appeared in public since.Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Wednesday that communication with Khamenei was "difficult at the moment"."In any case, his presence is a very great source of strength for us so that we can continue," Pezeshkian said, according to state media.The younger Khamenei, who did not appear at his father's funeral ceremonies last month, has communicated through written statements but his low profile has led to speculation about his relations with other top officials.Pezeshkian insisted he had been able to hold productive meetings with him and been met with "kindness and very sound logic"."Unfortunately, the current situation allows some malicious people to describe him differently and to present a different image of him," he said.

schema.headline: Iran says deal with Oman on Strait of Hormuz is 'in final stages'

title: Man charged with killing Scottish aid worker in Greece
description: An Afghan boxer has been charged with killing Scottish aid worker Elisabeth Ross in Greece.Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, has been charged with homicide with in
body: An Afghan boxer has been charged with killing Scottish aid worker Elisabeth Ross in Greece.Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, has been charged with homicide with intent, alongside robbery and weapons offences.The body of Ross, who was 38, was discovered in a suitcase by a homeless man in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of the Greek capital on 18 July.Ahmadzai was remanded in custody until his trial, which could take up to 18 months. During the hearing he asked for an English translator but did not respond to the charges.Ahmadzai arrived in court in Athens on Thursday morning in an unmarked Grey car. He was escorted out with masked officers holding his head down.On Wednesday, he was assigned a court-appointed lawyer and given time to prepare his defence.Ahmadzai was initially detained on illegal weapons possession charges and is facing a charge of homicide with intent, as well as allegations that he stole more than €10,000 (£8,500) from the victim's bank accounts using her bank cards. Homicide with intent is equivalent to a murder charge in Scots law.A statement from the police's organised crime directorate said Ahmadzai was brought to a police station on 30 July. "In particular, it emerged that the 26-year-old placed the body in a suitcase and transported it to the abandoned site," the statement said.The BBC understands he denies the charge of murder but admits moving the body, claiming that he did so because he feared he would be blamed for her death.

schema.headline: Man charged with killing Scottish aid worker in Greece

title: Nadia Sawalha threatens legal action against ITV over Loose Women removal
description: Loose Women panellist Nadia Sawalha has threatened to take legal action against ITV, claiming the network dropped her for speaking out in support of P
body: Loose Women panellist Nadia Sawalha has threatened to take legal action against ITV, claiming the network dropped her for speaking out in support of Palestinian rights.A legal organisation representing her has sent a pre-action letter to ITV, claiming the broadcaster "subjected Nadia to direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and harassment because of her protected philosophical beliefs".In an Instagram video, external, Sawalha said she had become "the target of an escalating campaign of smears, complaints, hostile media coverage and targeted calls to have me removed from Loose Women".She added: "Since then, ITV have taken me on and off Loose Women a number of times." BBC News has asked ITV for comment.The presenter said she "began speaking publicly in support of Palestine in December 2023", two months after the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel and Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza.She said she was "speaking out against brutal oppression", but her critics have accused her of promoting false claims and conspiracies about Israel and Jewish people.A group of Jewish executives in the entertainment industry recently sent a dossier to ITV, urging the channel not to reinstate her, citing what they called "repeated examples of conspiratorial rhetoric, inflammatory commentary, disinformation, and antisemitic discourse".Sawalha said she hadn't had a chance to see the document and answer the accusations, but has denied antisemitism.Two newspapers that previously accused Sawalha and her husband of antisemitism and supporting terrorism have since issued apologies and paid damages, external to the couple.In her video on Thursday, Sawalha said she had "mostly been told" by ITV that "the reason for [my removal] was, and I quote, 'It's all a bit noisy out there for us'."The controversy, she alleges, prompted ITV to remove her on repeated occasions from the line-up of its long-running lunchtime programme."ITV have continued to take me on and off Loose Women, forever changing the goalposts whilst also saying they couldn't guarantee they wouldn't take me off again as it would depend on what was said," she said.Sawalha added that she was "hired for being an opinionated woman on a discussion show and I've never brought up or spoken about Palestine directly on the show".The presenter also said she wanted to express "how sad I am that it's got to this - believe me, I have appealed to ITV's hearts and minds, but to no avail".The European Legal Support Center (ELSC), external, which supports pro-Palestinian cases, has written to ITV on her behalf, alleging she has been discriminated against because of her "anti-Zionist beliefs, which are protected under the Equality Act 2010".Sawalha has appeared regularly on the daytime panel show, which sees four female media personalities discuss topical subjects, since 2013.She also had an earlier stint on the panel between 1999 and 2002, shortly after playing Annie Palmer in EastEnders.Her other TV credits include Casualty and The Bill, and she is also a former winner of Celebrity MasterChef.

schema.headline: Nadia Sawalha threatens legal action against ITV over Loose Women removal

title: Car washes and vape shops can still sponsor skilled foreign workers despite visa changes
description: More than 1,900 small high street businesses including mini-marts, vape shops and car washes are licensed to sponsor foreign workers under a specialis
body: More than 1,900 small high street businesses including mini-marts, vape shops and car washes are licensed to sponsor foreign workers under a specialist scheme intended for high-earning individuals despite visa rules being tightened, BBC Verify has found.The Home Office scheme allows registered employers to recruit workers from overseas who meet a certain skill level. The rules were tightened in July 2025 to restrict the scheme mostly to graduate-level employees who would be earning at least £41,700.But a year on from the rule change, BBC Verify has found more than 1,500 grocery and convenience stores, 150 taxi operators, 100 barber shops, and dozens of car washes and vape shops are still on the register and able to sponsor people to apply for visas.More than 100 of those businesses were added to the skilled worker sponsorship list after the rules were tightened. Being on the register does not mean applications for individual visas would be approved.Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said on Thursday the government will "make sure that the rules are being properly enforced because we cannot have employers getting round the rules or finding different ways to deviate".Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered an urgent review into the presence of vape shops, barbers and car washes on the skilled worker sponsor register two months ago, following concerns over the "potential misuse of the system". The Home Office said at the time that any businesses seeking to abuse the system would have their licences revoked.A Home Office spokesperson said: "We have raised the skilled worker threshold and over 100 occupations are now ineligible for new skilled worker visas."It is understood some of the companies that joined the register after the rules changed may have applied before they took effect. Some companies may have also remained on the register because they were approved before July 2025 or are sponsoring workers who were already in the UK.There are more than 120,000 businesses with licences to sponsor skilled workers. The skilled worker scheme was introduced after Brexit for employers to recruit workers after EU free movement ended. Smaller firms must pay a £611 fee to apply to join the register while larger businesses, such as those with more than 50 staff, pay a fee of £1,682. Anyone can be visited by the UK Visas and Immigration service during the application process.Until July last year, someone being hired from abroad could qualify for sponsorship if their qualifications met an A-Level or equivalent standard, as long as they were paid at least £38,700 in most cases. Since the rule change, non-graduate professions, such as shop managers, are no longer eligible to apply. There are also higher English-language skill requirements that were introduced in January this year.The Home Office said there were 68,067 skilled worker visas granted in the 12 months to March this year - 29,745 to main applicants and 38,322 to their dependants - which is 30% lower than the year before. IT professionals were the most common type of people to be granted the visas, followed by those people working in finance, while the fall in approvals was mostly attributed to those in food preparation and hospitality trades no longer qualifying for the scheme.Jobs including sales and retail assistants, taxi drivers and chauffeurs are currently listed by the government as ineligible for skilled worker visas, but there are some exemptions, such as  bricklayers, carpenters or nursing assistants and other occupations where there is a shortage in the UK.The Home Office revoked 3,299 licences in 2025 compared with 347 in 2023. Its register does not state how many certificates of sponsorship or visas have been issued for each business or what type of role it has hired for, but Home Office guidance states firms must offer genuine jobs that meet skill and salary rules, and only sponsor workers for eligible roles.As businesses are only listed by name, it is not always clear what industry a company operates within. BBC Verify identified the more than 1,900 small high-street businesses that had retained a sponsorship licence by matching their names and locations to Companies House records and Google business listings to identify whether the mini marts, car washes and other small operations were on the list, and by analysing company names.Around 1,700 of those were in England, more than 140 were in Scotland, over 80 were in Wales and just two were in Northern Ireland.Separately, BBC Verify found 60 businesses on the register that had been fined for employing illegal workers between April 2024 and December 2025. They had been fined a combined £2.5m.A Home Office spokesperson said: "Illegal working will not be accepted, and businesses who face two or more illegal working penalties of up to £60,000, or fail to pay a penalty the first time, will have their license to hire workers revoked."Speaking about the visa rule change, Dr Madeleine Sumption, director of the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory, said that if businesses were on the register before the rules changed, they can continue to employ people they had already sponsored. "But they can't now bring in a new person to do those jobs."Toby Way, a lawyer at WestBridge Business Immigration which helps businesses apply to be sponsors, told BBC Verify that while most sponsorship approvals are legitimate, "We come across a lot of exaggeration and some downright lying about sponsored roles"."Hotels and restaurants have been hit massively by the rule changes. They're now unable to sponsor a chef or a manager, but they might claim they need someone for marketing or book-keeping, because those roles are on the temporary shortage list," he said."We know the Home Office looks at the finances of the businesses now and whether their revenue or profit means they can pay the required salary."Immigration lawyer Joanna Hunt of DAC Beachcroft said that it would be difficult for a high street shop to justify sponsorship at the degree level."Subject to a few exceptions, a job needs to be skilled to 'degree level' to allow a business to sponsor a worker to fill it and the Home Office will consider if the role fits with the type of business the sponsor operates. A high street shop may find this requirement difficult to demonstrate."Additional reporting by Rob England and Libby Rogers

schema.headline: Car washes and vape shops can still sponsor skilled foreign workers despite visa changes

title: England recall Pope and Lawrence for Pakistan Tests
description: Surrey duo Ollie Pope and Dan Lawrence have been recalled to the England squad for the first two Tests against Pakistan.The pair have been named in a
body: Surrey duo Ollie Pope and Dan Lawrence have been recalled to the England squad for the first two Tests against Pakistan.The pair have been named in a 16-man squad before the series opener at Headingley on Wednesday 19 August but Jacob Bethell will miss the entire series through injury, with Jordan Cox to be promoted to number three.The three-match series marks England's first Test outing since the retirement of captain Ben Stokes and sacking of head coach Brendon McCullum.Joe Root will captain the side for the first time since being reappointed to the role in July, with Marcus Trescothick serving as interim head coach. McCullum's replacement, Stephen Fleming, will begin his tenure against South Africa in December.———————————————————England's 16-man squad for the first two Tests against Pakistan: Joe Root (c), Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, Shoaib Bashir, Harry Brook, Brydon Carse, Sam Cook, Jordan Cox, Ben Duckett, Matthew Fisher, Emilio Gay, Dan Lawrence, Ollie Pope, Ollie Robinson, Jamie Smith, Josh Tongue.———————————————————Lawrence, who earned the last of his 14 Test caps in September 2024, is rewarded for his domestic form. The 29-year-old is the second-highest run-scorer in Division One of the County Championship, with 788 runs at 65.66, including five centuries, in 13 innings.He is slated to bat at six, filling a middle-order vacancy created by Stokes' retirement, but is far from a like-for-like replacement for the former captain.Only Gus Atkinson (79 wickets) has taken more Test wickets for England than Stokes (78) since the start of June 2022. Lawrence, who bowls right-arm off-spin, has taken nine wickets from 178.2 overs in the County Championship this season.There is no place in the squad for Sam Curran or Rehan Ahmed, who had both been tipped to replace Stokes."We have selected a squad for the first two Tests that balances rising talent with the experience needed against a quality Pakistan team," said England's men's national selector, Marcus North."Sam Curran is a player of real value and interest in terms of that role. He's had a heavy summer workload and he's been playing at the highest level with a number of niggles and we don't feel he's quite right at the moment for this Test squad."Rehan has done nothing wrong - he's someone we highly regard. At this stage we felt that going in with what we see as our best six batters with Smudge [Jamie Smith] at seven is key. That's why Lawrence has got the nod at six."Former vice-captain Pope was replaced by Bethell at number three for the final two Ashes Tests in Australia following an extended period of poor form and was subsequently dropped from the squad against New Zealand.Like Lawrence, he has performed well in the County Championship, scoring 510 runs at 56.66, including five 50+ knocks, for Surrey, but will not automatically slot back into the side in Bethell's absence.Bethell suffered a knee injury during the ODI series against India in July and is set to be replaced by Cox, who made his Test debut against New Zealand at The Oval.Essex's Sam Cook returns to the squad for the first time since last summer. The 29-year-old seamer made his international debut against Zimbabwe in May 2025 and was named in the squad for the five-match series against India but did not feature.Brydon Carse returns after a broken wrist ruled him out of the Indian Premier League and the start of the Test summer while England are sticking with spinner Shoaib Bashir, who featured in the first and third Tests against New Zealand after being overlooked during the Ashes.North also confirmed new head coach Fleming was involved in selecting the squad despite not taking over the role formally until after the Pakistan series."Stephen Fleming was involved in a lot of discussions," said North. "I think that was really important."Certainly from my perspective, as soon as he got appointed, I reached out and we had long conversations. It was important that our selection reflects the strategy and thinking long term moving into the winter when Stephen takes over the team."North was also asked about the prospect of former captain Stokes reversing his international retirement."Ben made the decision to retire and it's great to see him playing well and enjoying his cricket at Durham," he said."But until he reverses that decision and does become available for selection my job is to look at the players that are, and make sure that we become a strong, competitive England cricket team and work our way up those Test world rankings."'No brave new world for England'Analysis by BBC cricket reporter Henry MoeranFor those who were hoping for a brave new world, there may be disappointment. This is a squad with plenty of familiar faces and no potential debutants.Ollie Pope and Brydon Carse return for the first time since the Ashes and Dan Lawrence is selected two years on from his last Test appearanceThe big question was who was going to replace Ben Stokes as the all-rounder but that isn't entirely obvious.There is no place for Sam Curran, James Coles or Rehan Ahmed, who is dropped, which means Lawrence might find his part-time spin plays a significant role.North was keen to emphasise the strength in depth in English cricket, despite the lack of fresh names in the squad. Curran is someone we can expect to see sooner rather than later as the all-rounder gap looks to be filled. As for Ollie Pope - dropped after a miserable Ashes - his selection is one of a supporting leadership role and back-up as opposed to likely selection: should England lose a senior batter to injury it would leave them painfully short of experience.Many have suggested Sam Cook doesn't have the pace to perform at Test level but his red-ball skill remains unquestionable - 27 wickets for Essex this year in just six matches is some record.

schema.headline: England recall Pope and Lawrence for Pakistan Tests

title: Sunshine to meal times: How to beat jet lag
description: Jet lag is what you feel when local time changes abruptly, but your body clock is playing catch up, says Dr Nina Rzechorzek, who leads research at the
body: Jet lag is what you feel when local time changes abruptly, but your body clock is playing catch up, says Dr Nina Rzechorzek, who leads research at the University of Cambridge on human brain temperature, sleep, and circadian rhythms."After rapid travel across several time zones, your internal biological time initially stays aligned with home while you are trying to sleep, eat, and function on destination time."That mismatch can cause disturbed sleep, daytime sleepiness, poor concentration, irritability, reduced performance, and digestive problems," she says.And jet lag is closely linked to what are called our circadian rhythms – the body's internal body clock."Almost all the cells in our body maintain their own 24-hour clock, which are synchronised by a master clock in the brain," explains Dr Anna Edmondson, of the Laboratory of Molecular Biology at the University of Cambridge."The master clock is set to environmental timing cues, one of the most important cues being daily cycles in sunlight and darkness. However, if the timing of the sunlight/darkness cycles suddenly change (you fly far east or west), then it takes several days for the master clock to adjust to the new time, leading to jet lag."So effectively, it's like your body is still stuck in the timezone of where you've just flown from."

schema.headline: Sunshine to meal times: How to beat jet lag

title: Eve Muirhead: Winter Olympic gold medal-winning curler revokes retirement
description: "But the competitive side of me never disappeared," she added. "The more time I spent around elite sport and curling, the more I began to wonder wheth
body: "But the competitive side of me never disappeared," she added. "The more time I spent around elite sport and curling, the more I began to wonder whether I still had something to give on the ice."I know how demanding the road to an Olympics is, but I am returning from a very different place. I feel refreshed, physically strong and excited by the challenge. I would not be coming back unless I believed I could perform at that level again."Muirhead's gold medal-winning team-mate Vicky Drummond is also returning to the sport to rival her - and a third member of that rink, Jen Dodds - in the GB Curling mixed doubles programme.Drummond, 32, says being part of the BBC Sport team in Cortina in February rekindled her passion for competing, and that she wants to show her young daughter Sophie that "becoming a mum doesn't mean your ambitions have to end"."More than anything, I want my return to mean something beyond the ice," said the intensive care nurse, who will partner Euan Kyle."I want Sophie to grow up knowing that it's never too late to chase something that excites you. If she grows up believing that anything is possible because she watched me try, then this journey will already have been worth it."I have no idea where this road will lead, but I'm excited to find out."

schema.headline: Eve Muirhead: Winter Olympic gold medal-winning curler revokes retirement

title: Farmer jailed for 'body in barrel' murder in Barnsley
description: A farmer who shot his lodger and dismembered his body has been jailed for 35 years.Richard Dyson, 55, disappeared in November 2019, but his remains, k
body: A farmer who shot his lodger and dismembered his body has been jailed for 35 years.Richard Dyson, 55, disappeared in November 2019, but his remains, kept inside a concrete-filled barrel in a trailer on a farm near Barnsley, were not discovered for nearly six years.A trial at Sheffield Crown Court heard how Christopher Wright killed Dyson when he tried to steal a gun from him before disposing of the body with the help of his childhood friend Karl Schwalbe.Last month, Wright, 73, was convicted of murder and Schwalbe, 72, was found guilty of perverting the course of justice. Wright, a former butcher, was also found guilty of conspiracy to pervert the justice, preventing a lawful burial and six firearms offences.Jailing him, Mr Justice Cotter said: "You had worked as a butcher and were skilled enough to do such a terrible thing, something few ordinary people would have the stomach for."Schwalbe was given a three-year sentence for perverting the course of justice.Bethany Dainty, Dyson's daughter, said her life had become a "living nightmare".She had issued numerous appeals for help tracing her father in the years he was missing.In a victim impact statement read to the court, she said: "Someone watched me suffering for years and said nothing. That level of cruelty is impossible for me to understand."The court previously heard Dyson had been living in his car outside Wright's cottage on Sheffield Road in Hoyland, often helping him with various jobs like cutting hedges, mending tractors and driving him to appointments.Jurors heard Wright was a "weapons fanatic" and "a collector", who owned a number of vintage firearms, old farm machinery and musical instruments.Dyson's ex-partner recalled how several months before his disappearance, Dyson had found a machine gun at Wright's farm and kept it because it was "worth a lot of money".Prosecutors said Wright became "greatly angered" when he found out about the theft and killed him "with a shotgun immediately to hand".The last call from Dyson's phone was made on 17 November 2019 and he was reported missing. Both Wright and Schwalbe, of Dike Hill, Low Harley, in Rotherham, were interviewed by police in the months after but denied knowing what had happened.The pair's trial heard how Wright had enlisted the help of his childhood friend Schwalbe to help him hide Dyson's body.In July 2025, a review of mobile phone data uncovered that Wright had called the owner of nearby Alderthwaite Farm in Hoyland three days after Dyson disappeared.Farmer Ian Ollerenshaw told the court Wright had asked if he could store a livestock trailer on his land while he was "tidying up" his own farm, and noted the events of that day in his diary.Ollerenshaw, who like Wright was a tenant of the Wentworth Estate, said the trailer was towed onto his land by a Fordson vintage tractor, but that he did not look inside it once it was parked.Dyson's body was later discovered in a concrete-filled barrel inside the padlocked trailer alongside Wright's ID.

schema.headline: Farmer jailed for 'body in barrel' murder in Barnsley

title: Shorts, strappy tops, sandals: Should you wear them in the office?
description: Shorts, strappy tops and sandals: What is acceptable to wear to work?Image source, Getty ImagesByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter Updated 1 hour agoYet an
body: Shorts, strappy tops and sandals: What is acceptable to wear to work?Image source, Getty ImagesByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter Updated 1 hour agoYet another summer heatwave could be on the way to make your commute sweaty and your workplace stuffy.What to wear to work in the summer can be a surprisingly difficult decision. Shorts, strappy tops and sandals may keep you cool - but will they be judged too casual, revealing or unprofessional?There's a bare-legged backlash in Tokyo where officials encouraged men to swap suits for shorts at work, prompting complaints about hairy legs in the office.So what is acceptable to wear to work, how can you successfully style your summer wardrobe and can your boss tell you what you can and can't wear?Figure caption, Should men be allowed to wear shorts in the office?Conor, who works in media, has regularly worn shorts to the office during the recent hot weather. "Who gives a monkey's what you wear?" he says. "If you're able to do your job safely, professionally and appropriately, there's a lot to be said for letting people be comfortable."And many seem to agree - a recent poll by market research firm Ipsos found 62% of adults thought it was acceptable for men to wear shorts to work in hot weather, while 63% said the same for women.But we aren't talking short-shorts or denim hot pants fashion designer Amanda Wakeley points out: "If you're asking yourself whether they're too short, they probably are".She says shorts are "the trickiest item to get right in a professional environment" and recommends tailored, longer shorts paired with a crisp shirt or lightweight blazer for both men and women.Stylist Clare Chambers agrees shorts should sit around the kneecap for both men and women. For men, she recommends tailored chino-style shorts with an untucked T-shirt or shirt.Sandals Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Socks and sandals are a combo hard to pull off at the best of times, let alone in the officeWakeley describes flip-flops as one of the few definite "no" items in most offices. "They instantly signal leisure rather than professionalism and can make even the most polished outfit feel underdressed," she says.Chambers agrees, and says even during the hottest weather, woven flats are a better option because they are breathable while still covering the foot.Almost two-thirds of people questioned by Ipsos said they were unacceptable for men in the workplace, while 58% said the same for women.Sandals, however, are a slightly different matter as Wakeley says refined leather sandals can be entirely acceptable in many offices, provided they are clean and well maintained.The difference, she says, is whether they look like part of a considered outfit or something that would normally be worn around a swimming pool.She adds that while socks and sandals have become a viral fashion trend "it's important to consider whether a trend aligns with the image you want to communicate professionally". "This combination can read as highly casual and youthful, which may unintentionally detract from giving you a credible and authoritative presence."Strappy topsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Public opinion is divided over bare shoulders at workSome 40% of adults considered tank tops or vest tops acceptable for women at work, compared with only 24% who said the same for men, according to Ipsos.Natasia, a teacher in London, says at a previous school she and other staff had been summoned "regularly in the summer months to tell us off about our outfits."She says she was also told to cover up her tattoos. "It should be OK to have your arms out at work especially when it's hot," she says.Wakeley says a well-cut camisole or strappy top can work when worn beneath a linen overshirt, lightweight jacket or tailored co-ord. On its own, however, it may feel too informal.Chambers says if you're wearing a strappy top "you must wear a strapless bra as it utterly kills an outfit when you can see bra straps".She explains that thicker straps are a safer option where the dress code is unclear and recommends satin camisoles as a more polished alternative to basic cotton vests.She adds that while bandeau tops are "such an on-trend look this summer, they are a no-go for work"."The constant need to keep fiddling to pull them up displays an uncomfortable and unconfident demeanour," she says.How to style summer clothes at workImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The answer to dressing for the heat isn't necessarily to wear less, but to choose clothes more carefullyWakeley and Chambers both say that you don't need to lose your personal style when dressing for the office and you can still inject plenty of personality while following a dress code. Here are their top tips on how to style summer clothes for the office. Can your employer tell you what to wear?Climate change is expected to bring more severe, frequent and longer-lasting heatwaves in UK summers in the coming years.Employers are allowed to set standards around clothing and appearance, particularly where there are legitimate reasons such as safety, branding or maintaining a professional image.But employment lawyer Sarah Tahamtani says dress codes should be "reasonable, proportionate and capable of justification"."During extreme heat, employers should consider whether existing requirements remain practical and whether greater flexibility can be introduced."They must also consider employees with disabilities, medical conditions or other vulnerabilities that may be worsened by high temperatures.An employee who believes a request is unreasonable or inconsistently applied should first raise the issue with a manager or HR and explain how the rule is affecting their comfort or ability to work safely.

schema.headline: Shorts, strappy tops, sandals: Should you wear them in the office?

title: Jason Arday: Cambridge professor in plagiarism row quits
description: Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row resignsImage source, Faculty of Education / Jason ArdayImage caption, A picture of Arday released when
body: Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row resignsImage source, Faculty of Education / Jason ArdayImage caption, A picture of Arday released when he was appointed a professor at CambridgeByCaitlin DohertyBBC NewsUpdated 7 hours agoA University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row has resigned "with immediate effect". On Wednesday the university said it had launched an investigation into Professor Jason Arday "following new information" about his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments". Arday - who became the university's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - has admitted errors in his work, but said he had faced "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack" and was not a "liar". It came after a series of media reports questioning some of his achievements and allegations of plagiarism in his PhD thesis. Arday said he had "concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".In the statement posted by the Good Law Project on Wednesday, Arday said that being appointed professor had been "without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life". But he added: "There comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great." He said his resignation should not "be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge. "Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me." Thanking his students and colleagues, he said that "for my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".Arday said "this is not the end of my work" and that he needed "time to heal". "When that time comes, I will return," he added. Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher and self-defined "race realist", whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".He claimed on Substack that he had put Arday's work through a plagiarism detection software, which found that "many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source".Cambridge had initially described allegations made against Arday as a "vile campaign to undermine his credibility".Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated allegations of plagiarism in his thesis that were made last year, but did not uphold the charges.The BBC has contacted the university for further comment.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jesus College, where Prof Jason Arday is a fellow, said it is launching its own process 'parallel' to the university's investigation into the professor.On Saturday, Arday told the Times in an interview, external that he was accountable for those mistakes, but that "what I am not is a liar".He told the newspaper: "There has been, since I arrived at Cambridge, a very well orchestrated and co-ordinated campaign to unseat me from my position."He suggested that this was "racially motivated" and that he had become a "lightning rod" for criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policy.Arday said some errors in his early academic work was because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information, and that similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics."We're talking about academia here. I didn't murder somebody. I think the cruelty that I've experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable," he told the newspaper.Cofnas had also questioned Arday's claims that he ran 30 marathons in 35 days, and 300 miles in three days for charity, which Arday said had raised more than £5m for charity, as well as running 600 miles on a treadmill in six days.Arday told the Guardian, external that the £5m was raised with the help of others over a 20-year period, but said he could not name these people as he had signed non-disclosure agreements.When asked by the newspaper about the 600 miles challenge, he said it was actually completed over a 12-day period to allow for rest days because of the "cumulative wear and tear of training" from previous challenges.He told the Times that he stood by the other running records."I can't make people believe me," he said. "Nobody lives their life having a receipt for every single thing they say or they've done."Earlier on Wednesday, the University of Cambridge said its inquiry had begun "following new information" about Arday's "academic qualifications and honorary appointments"."Separately, there remains a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct, which are being handled in line with our Misconduct in Research policy," the university said in a statement.It added: "While we are fully aware of the public commentary and concerns around this matter, it remains vital that any process is thorough and adheres to both university policies and employment law."We also fully recognise that there is a person at the centre of this situation, and we continue to provide support to him." Jesus College, where Arday is a fellow, has said it is launching its own process "parallel" to the university's investigation.Earlier on Wednesday, publisher Simon & Schuster - which is set to publish Arday's memoir later this month - defended Arday in a statement to AFP news agency."We are proud to publish Professor Jason Arday. We have worked closely with him... and can speak to the professionalism and integrity he has brought to every stage of the publication," Simon & Schuster said.Separately, the Metropolitan Police confirmed it had investigated a journalist over an allegation of harassment after he emailed questions to Arday, before concluding no offence had been committed.The force acknowledged asking the journalist to make no further contact with Arday was not the right action to have taken and had the potential to frustrate legitimate journalism.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Academic Kehinde Andrews said what was underlying the whole furore is that black people do not belong in institutions like Cambridge.'No benefit for black people'The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within the academic community, with some arguing the universities are as culpable as Arday.Kathleen Stock, a philosopher and former Professor at Sussex University, said Arday's hire was motivated by the universities being "desperate for good press"."The elite universities like Cambridge and Oxford had a particular problem because they are perceived to be quite harsh places, quite unkind places and very white places. And they wanted to change that impression," she told the BBC's Today programme.Stock, who resigned her post in 2021 amidst a campus row over freedom of speech and her views on gender identity, said this was a "watershed" moment.She claimed universities "pretended not to see the gaps, or maybe just didn't see the gaps because they're hopelessly naive or desperate for good publicity in a way which obscures every other thought".But Kehinde Andrews, an academic and author who was previously at Birmingham City University, said the idea that black academics had an advantage because of their racial background was not true.He told the BBC's Today programme: "What happens to black academics, is we're not in an area where it's great and the left wing universities love us and they're trying to promote us. What happens is you work at a place for 12 years, you're very, very successful, and then you get made redundant. That's the experience of black academics."For three years they've been trawling through all of this to prove that there's some conspiracy to benefit black people, and I am a case in point that will tell you there is no benefit for black people in higher education, it is almost impossible to get jobs like that at Cambridge."Jovan Owusu-Nepaul, who describes himself as an associate of Arday, told BBC Newsnight on Wednesday that he found "the whole thing regrettable"."From, I think, how he's been treated and the quite obtuse spotlight on him about his CV - career - at Cambridge University," he said. "I think it's also regrettable that there may be some untruths that have come out about his CV."He said it was "appropriate" to respect Arday's request for "a bit of space".

schema.headline: Jason Arday: Cambridge professor in plagiarism row quits

title: Majority of England's rivers and lakes fail pollution review
description: The government is already on course to miss its legally binding target of restoring 77% of England's waters to good ecological status by 2027 - a goal
body: The government is already on course to miss its legally binding target of restoring 77% of England's waters to good ecological status by 2027 - a goal the environmental watchdog, the Office for Environmental Protection, has warned will be missed by a "considerable margin".It's now investigating both the government and the Environment Agency over possible rule breaches.Environment Secretary Angela Eagle said the figures "underline the need for wholesale change across the water sector".She pointed to new laws the government has introduced to hold water companies to account and record investment. "We will drive forward a system that puts the public interest first," she said.Much of the debate about the state of England's waters has centred on water companies and the sewage they release into rivers. But campaigners and scientists also point to agriculture as an equally large source of pollution - one that attracts far less public attention.Erica Popplewell, of the campaign group River Action, said some farming, particularly intensive poultry units - vast sheds housing hundreds of thousands of birds - were a growing threat to rivers such as the Wye and Severn."There's a lot of poo that comes out of the chickens," she said. "If it goes straight into a river, it causes eutrophication. The whole ecology of the river is damaged, and the river is dying." She called on the government to tackle sewage and farming "with the same urgency".The National Farmers' Union of England and Wales has been approached for comment.Other types of pollution affecting England's bodies of water, the Environment Agency pointed to, include petrol, garden pesticides and contaminated water running off roads picking up microplastics.The Environment Agency stressed that this year's data could not be directly compared with 2019 because it had changed its methods.In particular, it said the steep fall in the number of lakes ranked as good - down about half from 2019 - largely reflected a change in how its experts now assess them, rather than a genuine decline in their condition.Its chair, Alan Lovell, acknowledged too many water bodies were "still not achieving the standards we want to see", adding that the agency was "transforming our enforcement work" with its largest ever workforce.But Prof Penny Johnes, a leading water quality scientist at the University of Bristol, told BBC News the true picture was almost certainly worse than the classifications suggested.The scheme was "not fit for purpose", she said, measuring too few pollutants too infrequently, and missing nitrogen and other substances scientists have long understood to be driving rivers' decline.The findings come as much of England sits in official drought, with rivers running low and more than 20 million people facing hosepipe bans. Lower flows can concentrate the very pollution the new data is designed to track, leaving fish and other aquatic life exposed to more dangerous levels. Hundreds of dead fish linked to heatwave and pollutionClimate change is expected to bring drier and hotter summers which could further exacerbate this issue. Asked directly whether England's waters were healthier than six or seven years ago, Prof Johnes said: "No, definitely not."Every river and lake failed the test for chemical pollution.The Environment Agency said this is because legacy substances, such as heavy metals from mining, take decades to break down, and some are building up. But Prof Johnes said it was also a "failure to regulate effectively" the new chemicals entering rivers, from antibiotics to the "forever chemicals" known as PFAS - many not routinely monitored.There are currently 23 enforcement notices against water companies requiring them to lower the levels of PFAS to reduce the danger to human health.Water UK, which represents the water companies, has called for PFAS use to be banned to limit their build-up and reduce water treatment costs, but the chemicals are currently used in thousands of products, from school uniforms to medical devices.It said it was spending record amounts of money on improving the country's waterways."Water companies are investing £22bn in environmental improvements by 2030. This will help to secure our water supplies, support economic growth and end sewage entering our rivers and seas."The Environment Agency also noted that other European countries are doing even worse in terms of the good health of their waterways, with only 8% in Germany and just 1% in the Netherlands.But Prof Johnes said such a comparison is misleading, because of varying methodologies across nations.

schema.headline: Majority of England's rivers and lakes fail pollution review

title: Are AI recruitment tools affecting mid-life women's careers?
description: 'I've had to Botox my CV': Are AI recruitment tools affecting women's careers?Image caption, Stacey Duguid believes AI-powered recruitment tools are d
body: 'I've had to Botox my CV': Are AI recruitment tools affecting women's careers?Image caption, Stacey Duguid believes AI-powered recruitment tools are disadvantaging mid-life womenByLondon work and money correspondentUpdated 4 hours agoThe fear of becoming surplus to requirements because of advancements in AI is one shared by millions of workers, but are AI recruitment tools posing a specific threat to women trying to return to employment?After a career spanning decades, with senior corporate roles in fashion, and a period of freelancing, 52-year-old Stacey Duguid decided to find "one last job". What followed was 16 months of sending "gazillions" of CVs, with little more than a handful of automated replies, despite never previously struggling to find work.Feeling "lonely and shameful" and wondering if it was a "me problem", she posted on social media asking whether other women her age were having the same experience. The response was overwhelming, with thousands of women saying they were facing similar struggles.Stacey, who lives in north London, believes AI-powered recruitment tools could be contributing to the problem and has "Botoxed" her CV by removing references to her age and experience."AI holds a mirror up to society. It's a reflection of our bias," she said."I'm not saying this is just a women's issue; I've had messages from men too. My point is about gendered ageism."Confidence 'taken a hit'The BBC has since spoken to more than 60 women aged 40 to 65 across a range of industries who have been struggling to find work.Most have decades of experience in senior roles and say they've submitted countless CVs, only to receive automated rejections or no response at all.Like Stacey, many believe AI recruitment tools are playing a role. Image source, Koeyli JalukaImage caption, Koeyli Jaluka says that after applying for more than 400 jobs, her confidence has "taken a hit"Koeyli Jaluka, 49, has held senior roles across manufacturing, corporate and healthcare."I've never been in this position before. For the last 10–12 years I've been headhunted. Now I'm hunting for jobs and being relentlessly rejected."Made redundant nine months ago, she's applied for 442 jobs and has heard back in only a few cases. She's occasionally been told she's "too senior" – which she believes is "code for old". Despite two decades of experience and two degrees, she says her confidence has "taken a hit".She believes tighter budgets, AI screening and increasingly narrow hiring criteria are all contributing."A lot of us have been told by career coaches to shave off the first 10 years of work on our CVs just to ensure we don't come across as having worked for too long."'I'm on jobseeker's allowance'Image source, Anna CowieImage caption, Anna Cowie says she's lost count of the number of CVs she's sentAnna Cowie, 52, had a 30-year career in advertising but has been unemployed for almost four years. She's lost count of the number of CVs she's sent, despite having never previously been without a job.After decades of working for big brands, most recently helping to launch the new Battersea Power Station, she's now on jobseeker's allowance. Anna has turned to volunteering for community festivals, and has found networking with real people a much more promising approach."You're seen as a human and not just lines on paper."'Huge repercussions'While it is impossible to know in many cases whether AI tools played a role in a screening or a rejection because employers rarely disclose details of their recruitment processes, there are widespread fears that AI recruitment tools are disadvantaging mid-life women, external.The City of London Women Pivoting to Digital Taskforce, which focuses on women in the financial and professional services sector, has raised concerns, external about the growing use of AI in recruitment and its impact on women.Chair Caroline Haines said the taskforce's research found significant concern that AI used to screen job applications and CVs does not recognise the skills many experienced women can bring.Image caption, Caroline Haines says there is concern that AI used in recruitment does not account for many women's skills"There is a high level of concern that AI at initial recruitment level... doesn't account for the skills of a vast body of women that could be very effective and therefore promote economic growth," she said.For example, women who have taken time out of work for childcare may have gaps in their CVs that some AI screening systems could interpret negatively.In terms of the bigger picture, the taskforce estimates AI and automation could displace hundreds of thousands of women's jobs by 2035. Using data from Market and skills projections: 2020 to 2035, Department for Education, external, the taskforce estimates that without significant investment in retraining, firms could face more than £750m in severance costs.   In the digital taskforce's recent survey, external of over 1,000 women, 68% said they had not been given the opportunity by their employer to retrain or transition into digital roles."When the country is desperate for economic growth, we need to use whatever resource we have, and the resource of women who are mid-career, mid-experience. If they drop out of the market there are huge repercussions," Haines said.Image caption, Laura Holden believes AI recruitment tools have the potential to cause "significant harm" The BBC understands that some London-based companies have stopped using AI tools for fear of bias in their recruitment. Laura Holden, an AI lawyer and founder of the Bonsai AI and legal consultancy, said companies often do not understand how the tools work, which has the potential to cause "significant harm".She argued it is difficult to determine whether there is bias because "there is a lack of regulation globally that requires providers to show how their tools work".She pointed to CV screening tools and AI-scored interviews as examples of where bias can emerge.One tool, she said, grades CVs from A to D, encouraging recruiters to prioritise higher-ranked candidates. Others flag factors such as a seven-year career gap as a "thing to note", potentially influencing decisions unfairly.Holden said providers were "very quick" to claim their tools are safe and reduce bias, while designing and marketing them in ways that encourage employers to reject large numbers of applicants based on AI-generated scores. Although companies describe them as decision-support tools, she said they often functioned as "automated decision-making systems".She called for mandatory testing and stronger regulation before AI recruitment tools are deployed, arguing existing laws were not designed with AI in mind.'Completely faulty' logicDr Eleanor Drage, a senior researcher at the University of Cambridge, said concerns about AI disadvantaging women in recruitment are "very justified". She argued that human recruiters were better able to recognise the value of candidates returning from career breaks, such as maternity leave, and the transferable skills they bring - qualities AI may overlook. While Drage said it was "very difficult" to prove AI recruitment tools are inherently biased, she argued the logic they operate by is "completely faulty" because they cannot assess a person's intrinsic value or personality in the way a human recruiter could. Figure caption, Stacey Duguid appeared on Tuesday's Woman's HourShe added that many recruiters do not fully understand how these tools work, and said companies should use AI to evaluate their own hiring practices rather than to assess "vulnerable populations, like older women going back into the workforce, or people who've had a career break".While Drage acknowledges the benefits of using the tools, including helping hiring managers identify candidates with similar characteristics to people who have previously been hired, she says often "they're not on the side of the jobseeker".'Rigorously tested'The concerns raised in this article by interviewees relate to the use of AI-powered recruitment tools more broadly and are not directed at any single provider.Workday, the maker of popular AI-powered human resources software, is facing claims, external that it violated Californian law thousands of times by ​weeding out job applicants at many major companies for discriminatory reasons.The case is proceeding, with a ruling expected later this year.The BBC contacted Workday, which said the claims in the suit were false, adding that its tools don't make hiring decisions. More generally, Workday highlights that its recruitment tools help recruiters identify candidates who best match a job description based on their skills and experience, supporting rather than replacing human judgement.The company said its AI was "rigorously tested" through its Responsible AI programme and "does not consider traits such as age or gender".Workday added that, when used responsibly, AI can help qualified candidates avoid "getting lost in the pile".Image source, Eleanor DrageImage caption, AI recruitment tools are often "not on the side of the jobseeker", according to Dr Eleanor DragePrime Minister Andy Burnham recently raised concerns about AI used in hiring, and that it hadn't made "recruitment fairer". A government spokesperson said: "While AI can help employers manage large volumes of applications and reduce administrative burdens, it is vital that recruitment processes remain fair, transparent and accessible. "Existing legal protections, including equality and data protection law, already apply to AI systems, and we will act where additional protections are needed."A spokesperson for Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan said AI presented both opportunities and challenges, particularly as women are more likely to work in AI-exposed roles. They said the mayor had backed recommendations from the London AI and Jobs Taskforce to help employers adopt AI responsibly and support workers through the transition.As for Stacey, she has set up a community chat and platform to help women feel less alone, and to help companies address the issues in question."I want us, as a group, to be heard and seen. And for gendered ageism to become a thing of the past."Because if we're lucky, we all get old."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, X and Instagram. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.ukGet in touchHave you been affected by the issues in this story? Share your experiences

schema.headline: Are AI recruitment tools affecting mid-life women's careers?

title: Reform UK pledges to reward public for illegal working tip-offs
description: Reform UK says it would pay members of the public for tip-offs that lead to successful prosecutions of High Street shops employing illegal workers if
body: Reform UK says it would pay members of the public for tip-offs that lead to successful prosecutions of High Street shops employing illegal workers if it gained power.The party's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said financial rewards under a "Turkish barbers tip line" would be paid from larger fines it would impose on firms using illegal employees.It has pledged to fine larger firms up to 10% of their global revenues, and imprison the bosses of companies employing illegal migrants.The Home Office said it was already increasing penalties for companies hiring illegal workers. A source within the department called some of Reform's proposals "empty posturing". Reform said that if it won the next general election, it would make chief executives and directors of large companies profiting from illegal workers personally and criminally liable.That would be regardless of their knowledge of workers' legal status. The party said this would be similar to the personal liability of senior managers for the financial misconduct of their firms under Financial Conduct Authority rules.Reform said it would also introduce a tip line for the public to report suspected illegal working or organised criminal activity.Speaking at a news conference to unveil the policy, Yusuf said Reform would make it a legal duty for local authorities to investigate every "credible report" they receive.He said the reward scheme would emulate a system in the United States that rewards whistleblowers with a share of fines imposed after successful prosecutions of serious financial crime.He added: "In terms of the exact percentage, that would be in the final legislation that we pass."Companies have a legal responsibility to verify that people they employ directly have the right to work in the UK. For agency workers, the responsibility lies with the agency to conduct the relevant checks.Last year the Labour government extended this requirement to self-employed contractors carrying out work on behalf of a company, as part of a bid to improve enforcement in casual jobs in the so-called gig economy.There are sanctions including fines of up to £60,000 per unauthorised worker, but Yusuf said there was a need to increase the scale of the penalties, adding they only presented a "minor inconvenience" for bigger firms.A Home Office source said of Reform's announcement: "The government is already doing much of this. The rest is just empty posturing."A spokesperson for the department added: "We are already closing the loopholes that allow illegal migrants to work in the UK by extending right to work checks to the gig economy and delivery sector. "Employers who break the law face severe consequences, including fines of up to £60,000 per illegal worker, business closures, licence revocations and prison sentences of up to five years."They added that since Labour came to power, Immigration Enforcement action has increased "to the highest level in British history, with illegal working arrests up by 83% and raids up by 77%."

schema.headline: Reform UK pledges to reward public for illegal working tip-offs
